passage: It's been two months since I, Keerthana, filled in the Class 11 form, and I still remember my hands shaking over it. Sahil sir had coached me for the maths olympiad for two years. "You're the first girl from this school to reach the national round," he'd told me more than once. "You're made for PCM." I ticked Humanities. For a week I avoided the maths corridor, sure he'd look at me the way my uncle did, like I'd wasted something. When he finally caught me at the gate, I blurted out my reasons: economics, the village surveys I wanted to do, the questions numbers alone don't answer. He was quiet for a moment. "I'd have picked differently for you. But these are good reasons, and they're yours." Now when we talk after school, I argue back sometimes. He seems to like it.

qa.q: Which stream did Keerthana tick on the Class 11 form?
qa.a: She ticked Humanities.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana avoid the maths corridor for a week?
qa.a: She feared Sahil sir's disappointment and expected him to look at her as if she had wasted something, so staying away felt safer.

qa.q: What turning point came at the gate, and what made it work?
qa.a: Keerthana gave her own reasons, and Sahil sir admitted he'd have picked differently but accepted them as hers; that respect let the bond grow more equal.

qa.q: How might Sahil sir feel now that Keerthana argues back after school?
qa.a: He seems to enjoy it, perhaps proud that the student he coached now thinks for herself, even if a small part of him misses steering her toward maths.

grounding: A teenage girl picks a different stream than her male mentor advised, dreads his disappointment, and finds he respects her reasons, making the bond more equal.

passage:
Mentoring log, Bhupen Das, biology.
14 June. Alka came to the lab at lunch, holding her stream form face down. She has worked with me on the frog-count project since Class 9, and I had assumed, and said aloud, that she'd take Biology. She told me she's chosen Arts, to study languages. She couldn't look at me while she said it, and her voice shook on the word 'sorry'. I felt a flash of disappointment and noticed it. I told her, "It isn't what I'd have picked. But you've clearly thought hard, and I trust your reasons." She looked up then. "Thank you, sir."
Next step: I've asked if she'll still help the Class 9s with the frog count, as a colleague rather than my student. She said yes, grinning.

qa.q: What project has Alka worked on with Bhupen since Class 9?
qa.a: She has worked on the frog-count project.

qa.q: What was Alka afraid of as she held her stream form face down?
qa.a: She feared disappointing Bhupen sir, who expected Biology; she couldn't look at him and her voice shook on 'sorry'.

qa.q: What did Bhupen sir do with his own flash of disappointment, and why does it matter at this stage?
qa.a: He noticed it rather than acting on it, then said he trusted her reasons, which let their bond become more equal instead of breaking.

qa.q: How might Bhupen sir see Alka now that she has chosen Arts?
qa.a: He seems to see her less as his student and more as a colleague whose reasons he trusts, which is why he asked her to help the Class 9s.

grounding: A male teacher's log shows a teenage girl choosing Arts over his advice, fearing his disappointment, and hearing that he trusts her reasons.

passage:
"Just tell him," Shalini whispered outside the staffroom. "He's not going to bite."
"He spent a whole year pushing me towards science, Shalini."
Himani went in. Prakash sir looked up from a pile of test papers.
"Sir, I've filled the form. I chose humanities. Not science."
He was quiet for a moment. Her stomach dropped.
"You know I thought science suited you."
"I know, sir. But I want to study how cities are planned. Geography, economics. I've read about it for months."
He put the pen down. "I would have chosen otherwise, but I trust your reasons."
"You're not disappointed?"
"A little surprised. Now tell me about these cities."
Himani sat down, and for the first time she didn't wait to be told where.

qa.q: Which stream did Himani choose?
qa.a: Humanities, not science.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when Prakash sir went quiet?
qa.a: She felt scared and anxious that he was disappointed in her, since he had pushed her towards science for a year.

qa.q: What turning point does Prakash sir's reply open up?
qa.a: By trusting her reasons out loud, he lets their bond become more equal, and she can now share her plans as her own.

qa.q: What is Prakash sir likely experiencing as Himani explains?
qa.a: He seems a little surprised and perhaps let down at first, but chooses curiosity and respect over pushing his view.

grounding: Shows a student choosing a different stream from her mentor's advice, fearing his disappointment, and hearing that he trusts her reasons.

passage:
I practised the sentence in the mirror for three nights. "Joshi sir, I've decided on commerce." He had coached me for the science olympiad since Class 8. He'd said I had a physicist's brain. My friend Ayesha kept saying, "It's your life, yaar," but it didn't feel like only mine.
When I finally said it, I stared at his shoes. I was sure I'd see that look, the one teachers give when a girl wastes her chances.
Instead he said, "I would have chosen otherwise, but I trust your reasons. Tell me them anyway?"
So I did, properly, like an equal. Looking back, that was the first conversation where I wasn't just his student. I'm Gopika, and I still text him on Teachers' Day.

qa.q: How many nights did Gopika practise the sentence?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: Why did Gopika stare at Joshi sir's shoes?
qa.a: She was afraid of seeing his disappointment, worried he would think she was wasting her chances.

qa.q: What did Joshi sir do well at this stage?
qa.a: He admitted he would have chosen differently but still trusted her reasons and invited her to explain them.

qa.q: How might Ayesha see Gopika's struggle before the talk?
qa.a: Ayesha seems a little impatient but supportive, believing the choice is simply Gopika's to make.

grounding: Shows a student fearing her mentor's disappointment when she chooses commerce, and the mentor trusting her reasons.

passage:
Mentor log, Saturday
Gopika came to the lab after the practical today and stood by the door for a while. Then she said, very fast, "Sir, I'm not taking biology. I'm doing arts. I'm sorry." Her hands were twisting the strap of her bag. I had advised biology for two years, and honestly my first feeling was disappointment. I didn't let that be the thing she saw. I told her, "I would have chosen otherwise, but I trust your reasons. And you don't owe me sorry." She let out a long breath. We talked for twenty minutes about literature courses, and she argued back twice, which she has never done before. I have asked her to bring her shortlist next week so we can look at it together.
Vikas, biology teacher

qa.q: How long did Vikas and Gopika talk about literature courses?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What does Gopika twisting her bag strap suggest?
qa.a: She was anxious and afraid her teacher would be disappointed, which is why she apologised so fast.

qa.q: What did Vikas choose to do with his own first feeling, and why did it help?
qa.a: Vikas kept his disappointment from being the thing Gopika saw and told her he trusted her reasons, so she felt free to argue back.

qa.q: What would change if Vikas had shown his disappointment openly?
qa.a: Gopika might have felt guilty or backed down, and the bond would have stayed teacher-over-student rather than more equal.

grounding: Shows a teacher's note on a student who fears his disappointment when choosing arts, and his trusting reply that makes them more equal.

passage:
Friday
I finally told Pankaj Sir. I'm taking commerce, not science. He has been giving me extra physics problems since Class 9, and he always says I have "a scientist's brain". I practised all week, and when I said it this afternoon my voice cracked anyway. I was sure he'd look disappointed, or worse, go quiet. He did go quiet for a bit. Then he said, "I would have chosen otherwise, Ritika. But you've clearly thought about it, and I trust your reasons." I nearly cried in the staffroom corridor. Uday was waiting outside and asked why I looked like I'd won a match. I said it felt like Sir had just started treating me as an equal. I still want to show him my economics projects. That's allowed, right?

qa.q: Which stream is Ritika taking?
qa.a: Commerce, not science.

qa.q: What was Ritika afraid of before telling Pankaj Sir?
qa.a: Ritika was nervous and afraid of disappointing Sir, after years of extra physics problems and talk of a scientist's brain.

qa.q: What did Pankaj Sir's reply do for the mentoring bond?
qa.a: By admitting he would choose differently but trusting Ritika's reasons, he made the relationship more equal instead of controlling.

qa.q: What might Pankaj Sir have felt during his quiet moment?
qa.a: He may have felt a pang of disappointment at losing a science student, then chosen respect for Ritika's own judgement.
